title: Rachit Chawla vs Gurdeep Singh Bhatia on 21 January, 2025
full_text: Rachit Chawla vs Gurdeep Singh Bhatia on 21 January, 2025 IN THE COURT OF SH. GAURAV KATARIYA:MM (NI ACT), DIGITAL COURT-01, WEST, TIS HAZARI COURTS : DELHI ____________________________________________________________________ CIS No. 294/2022 PS Rajouri Garden U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act Rachit Chawla S/o Sh. Ramesh Chawla R/o H. No.B-32, Vishal Enclave, Near Rajouri Garden, New Delhi-110027 ........................ COMPLAINANT Vs. 1. Gurdeep Singh Bhatia S/o Sh. Lachhman Singh Bhatia R/o RZ-359, D-200, Gali No.16, Sadh Nagar, Palam Colony, Palam, Delhi-110045 2. Amandeep Kaur Bhatia W/o Sh. Gurdeep Singh Bhatia R/o RZ-359, D-200, Gali No.16, Khola Chowk, Sadh Nagar, Palam Colony, Palam, Delhi-110045 .......................... ACCUSED Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI ANKIT Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:35:23 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 1 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act JUDGMENT 1) Offence complained of : Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 2) Plea of accused : Pleaded not guilty 3) Date of institution of the case : 19.01.2022 4) Final order : Convicted 5) Date of reserving of order for judgment : 22.11.2024 6) Date of final order : 21.01.2025 Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:35:30 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 2 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act Brief reasons for decision: 1) Shorn of unnecessary details, the facts of the case are that the accused no.1 Mr. Gurdeep Singh Bhatia and accused no.2 Mrs. Amandeep Kaur Bhatia, are husband and wife and residing at RZ-359, D-200, Gali No.16, Sadh Nagar, Palam Colony, Palam, Delhi-110045. That accused no.1 and 2 are very well known to complainant, as accused no.1 has the friendly relationship, (qua), very good visiting terms with the complainant. Hence, complainant is very much well known to both of the accused persons. That accused no.1 alongwith the accused no.2 on dated 20.07.2020, approached the complainant and requested for the financial help/friendly loan of Rs.8,00,000/- by stating some urgent personal needs of theirs, due to financial hardships/financial constraints suffered by them and assured the complainant to return the same, by on or before 20.12.2021. That the complainant, after considering their request, being well known to both of the accused persons, friendly relationships (qua), visiting terms had agreed to give the friendly loan and accordingly gave Rs.8,00,000/- in cash to the accused no.1 on dated 20.07.2020. The accused no.2, being as the wife of the accused no.1 stood guarantor and the accused no.1 and 2, while admitting their joint legal liability and with a view to discharge the aforesaid legal liability, had issued and handed over a post dated cheque Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:35:36 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 3 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act bearing no.532537 dated 20.12.2021 for the sum of Rs.8,00,000/- drawn on State Bank of India, Palam Colony, Delhi Branch, in favour of complainant. At the time of issuance of said cheque, the accused no.1 and 2 further assured that the said cheque would be encashed on its due date and on presentation. That while receiving the said amount from complainant, the accused no.1 and 2 had also executed a proper receipt and promised, undertook and gave the assurance for the repayment of the said loan amount of Rs.8,00,000/- to complainant, by on or before 20.12.2021. 2) That, thereafter, on dated 20.12.2021, as per the assurance, as well as per the directions of the accused persons, when the complainant presented the aforesaid cheque bearing no.532537 dated 20.12.2021 for the sum of Rs.8,00,000/- drawn on State Bank of India, Palam Colony, Delhi Branch to his banker namely HDFC Bank, Branch B-6, Vishal Enclave, new Delhi, for encashment then the said cheque was returned dishonoured with remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide cheque return memo dated 22.12.2021 and intimation regarding the same was received by complainant on dated 27.12.2021 through courier. 3) Thereafter, being aggrieved from the act of both the accused persons and on receipt of return of cheque from bank, the complainant sent a legal demand notice dated 29.12.2021 to both the accused persons which was duly served Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI ANKIT Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:35:41 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 4 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act upon both the accused persons through speed post. Despite the service of the legal notice, the accused has not paid the cheque amount within the stipulated period of 15 days as per NI Act . Thereafter, complainant has filed the present written complaint case u/s 138 r/w 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 . 4) Cognizance of offence under section 138 NI Act was taken against the accused persons and summons were issued. Upon appearance, notice under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was framed against the accused no.1 and 2 during the course of proceeding dated 13.05.2022 to which the Accused no.1 and 2, inter alia, pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. It is stated by the accused no.1 and 2 that the cheque in question bear their signatures. It is stated by the accused no.1 and 2 that they have received the legal demand notice in question from the complainant. It is stated by the accused no.1 and 2 that the cheque in question has been issued from their account. 5) It is pertinent to mention that despite opportunity granted to lead the complainant's evidence, the complainant did not lead the evidence and vide order dated 21.01.2023, the right of the complainant to lead evidence was closed. Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:35:46 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 5 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 6) Thereafter memorandum of statement of accused no.1 and 2 u/s 313 Cr.P.C. r/w Sec 281 Cr.P.C . was also recorded in the case. It is stated by accused no.1 that he approached the complainant company for loan, however, he did not take loan from the complainant company. It is stated by accused no.1 that at the time when his loan was sanctioned, the complainant took some cheques from him and from his wife. Thereafter, the complainant asked him to visit to his office and gave a loan of only Rs.2,00,000/-. It is stated by ac- cused no.1 that the complainant assured him that he would give rest of the loan amount later as he is facing financial problem. It is stated by accused no.1 that he had given signed blank cheques and the same have been mis- used by the complainant and a false case has been instituted against him. It is stated by accused no.1 that he had also lodged police complaint regarding misuse of his cheques. It is stated by accused no.2 that the complainant promised to arrange a loan of Rs.15 Lakhs and took blank cheques. It is fur- ther stated by accused no.2 that the complainant only provided loan of Rs.2 Lakhs and he deducted the interest amount and he only received Rs.1,64,420/-. It is further stated by accused no.2 that the cheque has been misused by the complainant and a false case has been filed against him. In this backdrop, the accused expressed his willingness to lead defence evidence. Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:35:50 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 6 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 7) It is pertinent to mention that despite opportunity granted to the accused to lead the defence evidence, the accused did not lead the evidence and vide order dated 19.04.2024, the right of the accused to lead defence evidence was closed. 8) Thereafter, Learned Counsels for both the parties made detailed final oral submissions on behalf of respective parties. 9) Ld. counsel for the complainant contended that the accused no.1 and 2 have admitted that the dishonoured cheques in question bear their signatures and legal presumption of consideration u/s 139 of NI Act would act against them as they have signed the cheque in question. 10) It is stated by accused no.2 that the complainant promised to arrange a loan of Rs.15 Lakhs and took blank cheques. It is further stated by accused no.2 that the complainant only provided loan of Rs.2 Lakhs and he deducted the interest amount and he only received Rs.1,64,420/-. It is further stated by accused no.2 that the cheque has been misused by the complainant and a false case has been filed against him. 11) This is the factual matrix of this case. Let us now examine the legal benchmark which is to be satisfied in order to constitute an offence under section 138 NI Act: Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:35:54 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 7 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act (i) That the persons must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of certain amount of money to another person from out of that account. (ii) That the cheque should have been issued for discharge in whole or in party of any debt or other liability. (iii) That the cheque has been presented to a bank within a period of three months from the date on which it was drawn. (iv) That cheque is returned by the bank unpaid because of the amount of money standing to the credit of account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account or any other reason. (v) That the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of said amount by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of the information by him from the bank regarding the return of cheque as unpaid. (vi) That the drawer of the said cheque fails to make payment of the said amount to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. 12) It is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied, that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence u/s 138 of NI Act. 13) As per section 114 , Indian Evidence Act, 1872 which is applicable to communication sent by the post, the court are to presume that in the Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:35:58 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 8 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act common course of natural events, the communication would have been delivered at the address of the addressee. Section 27 of the General Clauses Act envisages that when a registered notice is posted, it is presumed to have been served unless rebuttal is given. 14) Final arguments addressed on behalf of both the parties have been heard and carefully considered along with the entire evidence on record. 15) In Kumar Exports Vs. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513, the Hon'ble Supreme Court, held as under: "The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the particular circumstances of the case the nonexistence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the Court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the nonexistence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI ANKIT Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:36:03 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 9 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act." 16) In M.S Narayana Menon Vs. State of Kerala , (2006) 6 SCC 39, the Apex Court dealing with the statutory presumption under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the N. I. Act inter alia held as under: Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:36:08 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 10 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act "29. In terms of Section 4 of the Evidence Act whenever it is provided by the Act that the Court shall presume a fact, it shall regard such fact as proved unless and until it is disproved. The words "proved" and "dis-proved" have been defined in Section 3 of the Evidence Act (the interpretation clause)...... 30. Applying the said definitions of "proved" or "disproved" to the principle behind Section 118(a) of the Act, the Court shall presume a negotiable instrument to be for consideration unless and until after considering the matter before it, it either believes that the consideration does not exist or considers the nonexistence of the consideration so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that the consideration does not exist. For rebutting such presumption, what is needed is to raise a probable defence. Even for the said purpose, the evidence adduced on behalf of the complainant could be relied upon. 32. The standard of proof evidently is preponderance of probabilities. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials on record but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. Therefore, the rebuttal does not have to be conclusively established but such evidence must be adduced before the Court in support of the defence that the Court must either believe the defence to exist or consider its existence to be Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI ANKIT Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:36:14 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 11 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act reasonably probable, the s standard of reasonability being that of the 'prudent man'." 17) It is a well settled proposition of law that once execution of Negotiable instrument is admitted, the presumption under Section 118(a) NI Act would arise that it is supported by a consideration. However, such presumption is rebuttable and the accused can prove the non-existence of a consideration by raising a probable defence. The burden upon the accused of proving the non-existence of the consideration can be either direct or by bringing on record the preponderance of probabilities by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. To disprove the presumption, the accused has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the consideration did not exist or its non- existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that it did not exist. 18) The gist of two above mentioned precedents is that the accused is in trial under Section 138 NI Act is left with two alternatives for his defence. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist for which direct evidence could be adduced which is seldom available or he can show by relying upon circumstantial evidence that under the particular circumstances Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:36:18 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 12 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act of the case the non-existence of consideration and debt is so probable that prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. It is evident that standard of proof to rebut the statutory presumption is not to prove it beyond the reasonable doubt as required in a criminal complaint. The onus to that effect on the accused is not onerous and what is required is a probable defence which could primarily find its foundation in preponderance of probabilities. In order to raise a probable defence, the accused can also rely on the evidence adduced by the complainant. However, a bare denial of the statutory presumption by the accused will not suffice. 19) In the present case, accused no.1 and 2 have admitted their signatures on the cheque in question. The defence of the accused as recorded in statement of accused is that they had approached the complainant for loan and had given the cheque in question as security to the complainant. The complainant had given a loan of Rs.2 Lakhs to them and had assured that the rest of the amout will be given later as he was facing financial problem. 20) No document whatsoever has been placed on record by the accused persons in support of the abovesaid contentions. The right of the accused to cross- examine the complainant was closed and nothing appeared on record to falsify the case of the complainant. DE was not led by the accused, Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI ANKIT Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:36:22 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 13 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act therefore, nothing fruitful could come on record through DE also. At the time of recording of SA, the accused persons have plainly said that they have taken a loan of Rs.2 Lakhs only and had given the cheque in question as security to the complainant. There is no evidence or document in support of their contention. The accused persons did not avail the opportunity of cross-examining the complainant, therefore, the version of the complainant could not be negated by the accused persons. Apart from that, there is a loan agreement placed on record by the complainant which clearly states that the accused persons had taken a loan of Rs.8 Lakhs from the complainant and had given two post dated cheques bearing no.523537 and 532538 dated 20.12.2021 for a sum of Rs.8 Lakhs each, both drawn on State Bank of India, Palam Colony. The accused persons have not denied their signatures on the loan agreement which further prograte the version of the complainant. 21) On the basis of the evidence and the documents, this court is of the considered opinion that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the presumption of Section 139 NI Act which lies in favour of the complainant. 22) There is a statutory presumption under section 139 of the act which arises in the favour of the complainant. This presumption is rebuttable and the accused is required to raise a probable defence. Burden of proof is hence Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:36:27 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 14 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act upon the accused in such cases. Reliance can be placed on the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of In M.S Narayana Menon Vs. State of Kerala , (2006) 6 SCC 39, the Apex Court dealing with the statutory presumption under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the N. I. Act inter alia held as under: "29. In terms of Section 4 of the Evidence Act whenever it is provided by the Act that the Court shall presume a fact, it shall regard such fact as proved unless and until it is disproved. The words "proved" and "dis-proved" have been defined in Section 3 of the Evidence Act (the interpretation clause)...... 30. Applying the said definitions of "proved" or "disproved" to the principle behind Section 118(a) of the Act, the Court shall presume a negotiable instrument to be for consideration unless and until after considering the matter before it, it either believes that the consideration does not exist or considers the nonexistence of the consideration so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that the consideration does not exist. For rebutting such presumption, what is needed is to raise a probable defence. Even for the said purpose, the evidence adduced on behalf of the complainant could be relied upon. 32. The standard of proof evidently is preponderance of probabilities. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials on record but also by reference to the circumstances upon which he relies. Therefore, the rebuttal does not have to be conclusively established but such evidence must be adduced before the Court in support of the ANKIT Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:36:31 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 15 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act defence that the Court must either believe the defence to exist or consider its existence to be reasonably probable, the s standard of reasonability being that of the 'prudent man'." 23) In the present complaint case, the accused has failed to rebut the presumption raised under section 139 of NI act that such liability do not exist. 24) The proposition of law which has been clearly explained in Bir Singh V. Mukesh Kumar dated 06.02.2019 and have been subsequently relied upon by the Apex Court and other Hon'ble Courts is as follows:- a. That the onus to rebut the presumption u/s 139 of the NI Act that the cheque has been issued in discharge of a debt or liability is on the accused and the fact that the cheque might be post-dated does not absolve the drawer of the cheque of legal consequences. b. That the bare reading of the provisions of Section 20 , Section 87 and Section 139 of the NI Act makes it amply clear that a person who signed the cheque and makes it over to the Payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption Digitally signed by ANKIT SOLANKI ANKIT Date: SOLANKI 2025.01.21 16:36:35 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 16 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act that the cheque had been issued for a payment of debt or in discharge of a liability. It has also been held that it is immaterial that the cheque may have been filed by any other person other than the drawer if the cheque has been duly signed by the drawer. c. Even if the blank cheque leaf voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption u/s 139 of the NI Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of any debt. 25) In view of above discussions, this court is of considered view that accused no.1 and 2 have failed to create a reasonable doubt over the veracity of story of complainant. It is noticeable that the complainant has to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt if the accused no.1 and 2 successfully discharge the burden placed upon them which the accused no.1 and 2 have failed to do in the present case. Digitally signed by ANKIT ANKIT SOLANKI SOLANKI Date: 2025.01.21 16:36:40 +0530 CIS No. 294/2022, PS Rajouri Garden Page No. 17 of 18 U/s. 138 Negotiable Instrument Act 26) In upshot of aforesaid discussion, I return finding of conviction of accused no.1 Gurdeep Singh Bhatia and accused no.2 Amandeep Kaur Bhatia for offence u/s 138 of NI Act in this case. 27) Let the copy of judgement be given free of cost to the convict Gurdeep Singh Bhatia and Amandeep Kaur Bhatia. 28) Let convict Gurdeep Singh Bhatia and Amandeep Kaur Bhatia be heard on quantum of sentence.
